## Objectives {#objectives}

By the end of this session you can:

- Define a label: a category assigned to each item, with a written
  definition for every category.
- Call a large language model from R through its provider's API and
  get answers back in a fixed format.
- Draw a hand-labeled sample with a seed and measure how often the
  model agrees with it.
- Read a confusion table to see which categories the model mixes up.
- Set up the pipeline so every result reproduces from saved responses.

## What we cover {#coverage}

- [Moreno-Medina et al. (QJE, 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjaf004)
  fine-tuned a small language model (trained it further on labeled
  examples) to sort 1.8 million TV news captions into crime and
  non-crime, hand-read a sample of the flagged stories, and measured how
  often police-killing coverage leaves out who fired.
  [Doh, Song & Yang (AEJ: Macro, 2026)](https://doi.org/10.1257/mac.20220312)
  fine-tuned a language model on the dovish and hawkish drafts Fed staff
  write before each meeting, then placed each actual statement between
  them to measure its stance. From finance,
  [Lopez-Lira & Tang (JFE, 2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104335)
  asked a large language model (a program trained on vast amounts of
  text that replies to written instructions) whether each headline was
  good, bad or unclear for the stock; the answers predict later returns.
- What a label is: the category assigned to one item, such as positive
  or negative for a sentence. The codebook you would hand a research
  assistant, a written definition of each category with a rule for the
  cases in between, becomes the prompt, the instructions plus the item
  you send to the model.
- Calling the model from R with `ellmer`: the API key stored in
  `~/.Renviron`, and a schema that fixes the output to one label per
  item from a set list. The running example: the same Federal Reserve
  statements labeled hawkish, dovish or neutral, set beside a dictionary
  score of the same text. Where the two disagree, your hand labels show
  which one is right.
- Verifying the labels against a hand-labeled sample. Draw it with
  `sample()` and a seed (a number that fixes the random draw), and label
  it before you see the model's answers. The agreement rate is the share
  of items where the model's label matches yours; 95% agreement tells
  you nothing when 95% of items share one label (the base rate). The
  confusion table, your labels as rows and the model's as columns, shows
  which categories the model mixes up, and the pattern usually points at
  the prompt.
- Whether the results reproduce: the model pinned (its exact version
  written once in one constant), every raw response cached to disk and
  committed, and the model and prompt named in the README. A fresh call
  can return a different label, and many current models offer no setting
  that stops this, so reruns read the cache and the numbers hold when the
  provider updates the model.
- Error analysis and the validation paragraph: sort the mistakes into
  kinds before choosing between a new prompt, new categories and hand
  coding, then write the methods paragraph that reports the model, the
  prompt, the sample, the agreement rate and the confusion table.
- In class: hand-label twenty items, compare them with the model, and
  report the agreement rate and the confusion table.
